lines.li: [us] Why does every sickhouse of yours keep a lamp over the door?
[them] For Aldith, who nursed a fever town alone through a whole winter.
[us] What happened in the spring?
[them] She hung the town's last lamp over the sickhouse door and let in anyone who came.
[us] Anyone at all?
[them] Raiders too, which is why the order has never asked since.
[them] We keep a book of everyone who walked out of our wards alive.
[us] Why keep the names?
[them] We were spared, and so we owe, and they're who we owe it to.
[us] It must be a long book by now.
[them] Long, and never long enough.
[us] What does a hospitaller fear?
[them] The fever coming back, and a door shut on someone sick.
[us] Not raiders?
[them] Raiders get sick too, and we take them in when they do.
[us] Why do your people never stay in one place?
[them] In the year the wells failed, a herd girl named Tamsa walked the last forty head north.
[us] Where to?
[them] To grass nobody believed in, and she brought every one of them home alive.
[us] And you've followed the grass ever since.
[them] The camps that followed her never stopped, so neither do we.
[them] A guest at our fire eats from the same pot as the elders.
[us] Even a stranger?
[them,likesus] A stranger once, and a friend after, as you are.
[them,!likesus] Especially a stranger, that's how they stop being one.
[us] Will it be a hard winter, do you think?
[them] The grass will tell.
[us] And what is the grass saying?
[them,winter] That we came down from the high ground just in time.
[them,!winter] That it's too early to say, which is what it always says.
[us] How did the league begin?
[them] At Harrow Ford, where the road belonged to whoever had the most rifles.
[us] What changed?
[them] Edda Vane asked every waymaster on the road for one guard and one wagon.
[us] And they gave them?
[them] Nine flags went through that ford together, and nobody fired.
[us] What do you mean by good ink?
[them] The Waystone Book writes fair dealers in black and robbers in red.
[us] Which are we?
[them,likesus] Good ink, and thick of it.
[them,!likesus] Neither yet, and the page is waiting.
[them] A word given at a waystone stands, whatever it costs.
[us] And if it costs too much?
[them] Then you shouldn't have given it, and you pay anyway.
[us] Who was the first pilgrim of your fellowship?
[them] Old Brannoc, a nearly blind preacher with a boy to lead him.
[us] Where did they go?
[them] To every holy place he had ever heard of, whoever's it was.
[us] And the doors on the way?
[them] He blessed every one of them, whether it opened or not.
[us] What are all the shells on your belt?
[them] One for every shrine I've reached.
[us] That's a lot of shrines.
[them,old] And a lot of years, and room on the string for one more.
[them,!old] Not yet, but there is no last shrine.
[us] What does a pilgrim fear?
[them] A shut door, a shrine nobody visits, and sitting still too long.
[us] Sitting still?
[them] The faith is carried on foot, so a pilgrim who stops is carrying nothing.
[us] How did the society begin?
[them] The night the old archive at Hesk burned.
[us] What was saved?
[them] Eleven books and a ledger, in a clerk's handcart.
[us] Only that?
[them] Ilse Varro copied them for the rest of her life, and we learned to read from her pages.
[them] A scholar's first oath is to copy one thing that would otherwise be lost.
[us] What did you copy?
[them] A farmer's almanac nobody else wanted, and I'm prouder of it than anything since.
[us] Is it true your people never stop asking questions?
[them] Strictly speaking, that's two questions.
[us] You see what I mean.
[us] How did the enclave come to be here?
[them] An ore hauler came down with a dead drive and no way back up.
[us] And the crew stayed?
[them] Its purser, Ines Okoro, sold the cargo, the passage and the debts, one bargain at a time.
[us] Until?
[them] Until the ships above were calling us, and they still do.
[them] Every bargain the enclave has struck is in the hauler's old manifest.
[us] Even the bad ones?
[them] Especially those, kept to the last digit like the rest.
[us] What does a broker fear?
[them] A debt nobody pays, and being stranded.
[us] You were stranded once.
[them] Nobody is stranded who has something to sell, and Okoro always did.
[us] Where do the river folk come from?
[them] From the night the dam broke and the valley towns drowned.
[us] How did anyone live through that?
[them] Wenna Reed's boats were on the water, and they pulled people off the roofs for three days.
[us] And those they pulled out?
[them] Stayed with the boats, and we count our families from them.
[us] Why are there so many knots in your nets?
[them] A knot for everyone ever pulled from the water by river folk.
[us] That's a heavy net.
[them] Heavy and lucky, the heavier the luckier.
[them] Never foul the water another drinks downstream.
[us] Is that a saying or a rule?
[them] On the river it's both, and the river folk keep it either way.
